s: The righteous will see God's destruction of the wicked man, fear, and laugh at him. They will say that he did not make God his strength but trusted in his riches and strengthened himself in his wickedness.

Chapter 53 is a psalm attributed to David, addressed to the Chief Musician and set to the tune of "Mahalath." It declares that the fool says in his heart there is no God, and that people are corrupt, doing abominable iniquity, with no one doing good. God looks down from heaven on the children of men to see whether any understand and seek him, and finds that everyone has gone back and become filthy together. The workers of iniquity are accused of lacking knowledge, eating up God's people as they eat bread, and not calling on God. They are then said to be in great fear where no fear was, because God has scattered the bones of the one who encamps against his people and has rejected them, and the psalm closes with a wish that the salvation of Israel would come out of Zion, so that Jacob and Israel would rejoice when God brings his people back from captivity.

God looks down from heaven on the children of men to see if any understand and seek him, and finds that all have turned back and become corrupt. He scatters the bones of the one who encamps against his people, puts them to shame, and rejects them. The psalm closes with the hope that he will bring his people back from captivity.
The fool says in his heart, "There is no God." He is described as corrupt and as having done abominable iniquity, with no one who does good.

The workers of iniquity are asked whether they have no knowledge, since they eat up God's people as they eat bread and do not call on God. They are said to be in great fear where no fear was, and God has put them to shame and rejected them.

God's people are consumed by the workers of iniquity, who eat them up as they eat bread. God defends them by scattering the bones of the one who encamps against them, and the psalm hopes he will bring them back from captivity.
Israel is named in the closing verse as the one whose salvation is wished to come out of Zion. When God brings back his people from captivity, Israel, along with Jacob, will be glad and rejoice.

The salvation of Israel is the object of the psalmist's longing in the final verse: "Oh that the salvation of Israel would come out of Zion!" It is linked to God bringing back his people from captivity, which would bring rejoicing and gladness.

Human corruption is portrayed as universal: every one has gone back and become filthy together, and there is no one who does good, "no, not one." God's looking down from heaven finds no one who understands or seeks him.

Chapter 54 is a prayer attributed to David, set in the context of the Ziphites telling Saul that David was hiding among them. David asks God to save and vindicate him by his name and might, and to hear his prayer. He describes strangers and violent men who have risen against him and do not set God before them. David affirms that God is his helper and sustainer, asks that evil be repaid to his enemies, and promises a free will offering and thanksgiving. He closes by declaring that God has delivered him from all trouble and that he has seen triumph over his enemies.

God is called on by David to save him by his name, vindicate him in his might, and hear his prayer. He is described as David's helper and the Lord who sustains his soul, and as the one who will repay evil to David's enemies and destroy them in his truth. David states that God has delivered him out of all trouble, and he promises to offer a free will offering and thanks to God's name, which he calls good.

David, identified in the heading as the author, prays for salvation and vindication after the Ziphites tell Saul he is hiding among them. He describes being attacked by strangers and violent men seeking his soul, and he affirms that God is his helper and sustainer. He vows a free will offering and thanksgiving, and declares that God has delivered him from all trouble and that his eye has seen triumph over his enemies.

The strangers are described as having risen up against David, and as violent men who seek after his soul. They are said not to have set God before them. David asks that God repay their evil and destroy them, and says he has seen triumph over his enemies.

In Chapter 55, a contemplation attributed to David for the Chief Musician, David prays to God in anguish over the oppression of the wicked, feeling terror and wishing he could fly away like a dove to the wilderness. He asks God to confuse his enemies, describing violence, strife, malice and lies within the city. He reveals that the deepest wound comes from a companion and familiar friend who shared sweet fellowship with him and walked with him in God's house, but who violated his covenant with smooth words that were really drawn swords. David calls for sudden death on his enemies, resolves to call on God morning, noon and evening, and urges others to cast their burden on the LORD, trusting that God will bring the bloodthirsty and deceitful down into the pit.

David prays in distress, pained and overwhelmed by terror, wishing he could fly away like a dove to the wilderness. He is betrayed by a close friend, calls for judgment on his enemies, and resolves to call on God evening, morning and noon, trusting that the LORD will save and sustain him.

God is asked by David to hear his prayer, confuse his enemies' language, and send death upon them. He is described as enthroned forever, as the one who redeemed David's soul in peace from the battle, who sustains those who cast their burden on him, and who will bring the bloodthirsty and deceitful down into the pit of destruction.

The enemies oppress David, bring suffering on him, and hold anger against him, prowling the city's walls with malice, abuse, threats and lies. David asks that death come suddenly on them and that they go down alive into Sheol, and states that God will hear and answer them; they never change and do not fear God, and they will not live out half their days.

The companion is a man like David and his familiar friend, with whom he once took sweet fellowship and walked in God's house. He has raised his hands against his friends and violated his covenant, with a mouth smooth as butter and words softer than oil that were really drawn swords, while his heart was war.
The city is where David has seen violence and strife. Enemies prowl on its walls day and night, and malice, abuse, destructive forces, threats and lies fill it and never leave its streets.

Chapter 56 is a poem by David, written for the Chief Musician to the tune "Silent Dove in Distant Lands," when the Philistines seized him in Gath. David asks God for mercy because his many enemies attack him all day, twist his words, and lurk to take his life. He repeatedly declares that he will trust God and not be afraid, asking what flesh or man can do to him. He asks God to cast down the peoples in anger, and notes that God counts his wanderings and keeps his tears. He closes by affirming that God is for him, promising thank offerings, and praising God for delivering his soul from death so he may walk before God in the light of the living.

God is asked by David to be merciful and to cast down the peoples in anger. He counts David's wanderings, puts his tears in a container and records them in his book, and is known by David to be for him. God has delivered David's soul from death and kept his feet from falling, and David praises his word and promises him thank offerings.

David, seized by the Philistines in Gath, cries to God for mercy because enemies oppress him all day and seek his life. He declares trust in God, says he will not be afraid, and praises God's word. He acknowledges vows to God, promises thank offerings, and credits God with delivering him from death so he may walk before God in the light of the living.

David's enemies are many and fight proudly against him, wanting to swallow him up and attacking and oppressing him all day. They twist his words, think evil against him, conspire, lurk and watch his steps, eager to take his life. David asks whether they shall escape by iniquity and says they will turn back on the day he calls on God.

David states that when he is afraid he will put his trust in God, and repeats that he has put his trust in God and will not be afraid. This trust is expressed in the question of what flesh or man can do to him. It rests on his knowledge that God is for him and on God's deliverance of his soul from death.

Chapter 57 is a poem by David, written when he fled from Saul and hid in the cave, set for the Chief Musician to the tune of "Do Not Destroy." David asks God for mercy and takes refuge in the shadow of God's wings until disaster passes. He describes himself as among lions and people whose teeth are spears and arrows and whose tongues are sharp swords. His enemies have set a net and dug a pit for him but fall into it themselves. David declares his heart steadfast, vows to sing and give thanks among the peoples and nations, and twice asks that God be exalted above the heavens and his glory be over all the earth.

God is called God Most High, the one who accomplishes David's requests, and David takes refuge in the shadow of his wings. He sends from heaven to save David, rebukes the pursuer, and sends out his loving kindness and truth. His loving kindness is said to reach to the heavens and his truth to the skies, and David asks that he be exalted above the heavens with his glory over all the earth.

David, who wrote the poem when he fled from Saul in the cave, asks God for mercy and takes refuge in him until disaster passes. He describes his soul as among lions and bowed down by enemies' traps, yet declares his heart steadfast. He resolves to sing praises, wake the dawn with lute and harp, and give thanks to God among the peoples and nations.

The enemies pursue David and are described as sons of men set on fire, with teeth like spears and arrows and tongues like sharp swords. They prepare a net for his steps and dig a pit before him, but they fall into the middle of the pit themselves. God rebukes the one who pursues David.

Chapter 58 is a poem by David, addressed to the Chief Musician and set to the tune of "Do Not Destroy." It challenges the "silent ones" and "sons of men," accusing them of plotting injustice and committing violence on the earth. It describes the wicked as wayward and lying from birth, with poison like a deaf cobra's that will not heed charmers. The speaker asks God to break their teeth, make them vanish like water, and be like a melting snail or a stillborn child. It ends with the righteous rejoicing at vengeance, and people saying there is a reward for the righteous and a God who judges the earth.

God is called on to break the teeth of the wicked in their mouth, and the LORD is asked to break out the great teeth of the young lions. He is described as sweeping away the green and the burning alike, and people conclude that he is a God who judges the earth.

The wicked are said to go astray from the womb, to be wayward and speaking lies from birth, and to have poison like a snake's, like a deaf cobra that will not listen to charmers. The speaker prays that their teeth be broken, that they vanish like flowing water, that their arrows be blunted, and that they be like a melting snail or a stillborn child. Their blood is where the righteous will wash his feet.
The righteous will rejoice when he sees the vengeance and will wash his feet in the blood of the wicked. Men will then say there is surely a reward for the righteous.
Vengeance is what the righteous will see and rejoice over, with the blood of the wicked washing his feet. It is taken as proof that the righteous have a reward and that God judges the earth.

Chapter 59 is a poem by David, written when Saul sent men to watch his house in order to kill him. David asks God to deliver him from bloodthirsty enemies who lie in wait for him though he has done no wrong. He asks God to punish the nations and the wicked traitors, and he describes his enemies as howling dogs who prowl the city at evening. He asks that they be scattered and consumed so that people will know God rules in Jacob. David ends by vowing to sing of God's strength and loving kindness, calling God his high tower and refuge.

David, in a poem tied to the time Saul sent men to watch his house to kill him, pleads with God for deliverance from bloodthirsty enemies, insisting he has done no wrong. He asks that they be scattered rather than killed so his people do not forget, and then be consumed in wrath. He closes by vowing to sing praises to God, his strength, high tower, and refuge, in the morning.

God is called on to deliver David, to rouse himself and punish the nations and the wicked traitors. He is described as laughing at and scoffing at the nations, as going before David with loving kindness, and as David's strength, shield, high tower, and refuge. David asks that his enemies be made to know that God rules in Jacob to the ends of the earth.

David's enemies are described as workers of iniquity and bloodthirsty men who lie in wait for his soul, gather against him without cause, and spew curses and lies, saying "who hears us?" They return at evening howling like dogs and prowling the city, wandering for food. David asks that they be scattered, caught in their pride, and consumed in wrath.

Chapter 60 is a teaching poem by David, set when he fought Aram Naharaim and Aram Zobah and Joab killed twelve thousand of Edom in the Valley of Salt. The speaker laments that God has rejected and broken his people, made the land tremble, and made them drink staggering wine, yet asks God to restore them. God is quoted as claiming Shechem, Succoth, Gilead, Manasseh, Ephraim, and Judah as his own, and declaring Moab his wash basin, Edom his to throw a sandal on, and Philistia a land over which he shouts in triumph. The speaker asks who will bring him into the strong city and to Edom, notes that God does not go out with their armies, and pleads for help against the adversary. The poem ends by affirming that through God the people will do valiantly and that he will tread down their adversaries.

God is accused of rejecting and breaking down his people, being angry, and making the land tremble, yet he is also asked to restore them and give help. He speaks from his sanctuary, claiming Shechem, Succoth, Gilead, Manasseh, Ephraim, and Judah, and promising triumph over Moab, Edom, and Philistia. The poem closes by affirming that he will tread down the adversaries.

Edom is named in the superscription as the nation of which Joab killed twelve thousand in the Valley of Salt. In God's speech he will throw his sandal on Edom, and the speaker asks who has led him to Edom.

God's people are described as rejected, broken down, shown hard things, and made to drink wine that makes them stagger. They are also given a banner by God for those who fear him, and are called his beloved. They express confidence that through God they will do valiantly.

l: Plea for restoration and deliverance, Psalms, Chapter 60
s: The poem opens by asking God to restore his people and mend the fractures of the quaking land. It continues by asking him to save with his right hand, answer, and give help against the adversary, since human help is vain. It ends with confidence that God will tread down the adversaries.

Chapter 61 is a prayer attributed to David, written for the Chief Musician and a stringed instrument. The speaker cries out to God from the end of the earth with an overwhelmed heart and asks to be led to a higher rock. He recalls that God has been a refuge and strong tower against the enemy, and he longs to dwell in God's tent and shelter under his wings. He affirms that God has heard his vows and given him the heritage of those who fear his name. The psalm asks for the king's life to be prolonged and for him to be enthroned before God forever, preserved by God's loving kindness and truth, and closes with a vow to sing praise daily.

God is called on to hear the speaker's cry and prayer, and is described as a refuge and strong tower from the enemy. He has heard the speaker's vows and given him the heritage of those who fear his name. He is asked to lead the speaker to the higher rock, to prolong the king's life, and to appoint loving kindness and truth to preserve the king.

David is named as the author of this psalm, which is addressed to the Chief Musician and set for a stringed instrument. As speaker, he cries to God from the end of the earth with an overwhelmed heart, and he expresses a wish to dwell in God's tent forever and take refuge under his wings. He recalls that God has heard his vows and resolves to sing praise to God's name forever and fulfill his vows daily.

The king is the subject of a request that God prolong his life so that his years last for generations. He is to be enthroned in God's presence forever, and God is asked to appoint loving kindness and truth to preserve him.

Chapter 62 is a psalm by David, addressed to the Chief Musician and Jeduthun, in which the psalmist declares that his soul rests in God alone as his rock, salvation, and fortress. He asks how long a group will assault him like a leaning wall, noting that they plan to throw him down from his lofty place, delight in lies, and bless with their mouths while cursing inwardly. He urges his own soul to wait in silence for God and calls on the people to trust God at all times and pour out their hearts to him. He declares that men of low and high degree are only a breath, warns against trusting in oppression, robbery, or riches, and closes by saying that power and loving kindness belong to God, who rewards each person according to his work.

God is described as the psalmist's rock, salvation, fortress, honor, strength, and refuge. He has spoken once, and twice it has been heard, that power belongs to him, and loving kindness also belongs to him. He rewards every man according to his work.

l: psalmist (speaker of the psalm), Psalms, Chapter 62
s: The psalmist, identified in the heading as David, declares that his soul rests in God alone and that he will not be greatly shaken. He is under assault and compared to a leaning wall, and he urges his soul to wait in silence for God, from whom his expectation comes.

l: assailants (those attacking the psalmist), Psalms, Chapter 62
s: The assailants are asked how long they will assault a man and throw him down like a leaning wall or tottering fence. They fully intend to throw him down from his lofty place, delight in lies, and bless with their mouths while cursing inwardly.

l: people (those urged to trust God), Psalms, Chapter 62
s: The people are told to trust in God at all times and to pour out their hearts before him, since God is a refuge for them. They are also warned not to trust in oppression, not to become vain in robbery, and not to set their hearts on increasing riches.
Salvation is said to come from God alone, who is the psalmist's rock and salvation. The psalmist's salvation and honor are with God, and this security means he will not be shaken.
The psalmist's refuge is said to be in God, who is also the rock of his strength. God is then declared to be a refuge for the people as well, who are urged to trust him and pour out their hearts.

Chapter 63 is a psalm attributed to David, written when he was in the desert of Judah. The speaker addresses God as his God, saying his soul thirsts and his flesh longs for him in a dry and weary land. He recalls seeing God's power and glory in the sanctuary, declares that God's loving kindness is better than life, and vows to bless and praise him, lifting up his hands. He remembers God on his bed in the night watches, says God has been his help, and that God's right hand holds him up. The psalm ends by declaring that those who seek his soul to destroy it will go into the lower parts of the earth, be given to the sword and become jackal food, while the king rejoices in God and the mouths of liars are silenced.

God is addressed as 'my God' and is earnestly sought by the psalmist, who thirsts and longs for him. He is described as having a power and glory seen in the sanctuary, a loving kindness better than life, and a right hand that holds the psalmist up. He has been the psalmist's help, and the king rejoices in him.

David is named in the superscription as the author of this psalm, written when he was in the desert of Judah. The speaker thirsts and longs for God in a dry and weary land, vows to praise and bless him while he lives, and lifts up his hands in God's name. He remembers God in the night watches, rejoices in the shadow of God's wings, and says God's right hand holds him up.

They are those who seek the psalmist's soul to destroy it. The psalm declares they will go into the lower parts of the earth, be given over to the sword, and become jackal food. It also says the mouths of those who speak lies will be silenced.

Chapter 64 is a psalm attributed to David, addressed to the Chief Musician. The psalmist cries out to God in complaint, asking to be preserved from fear of the enemy and hidden from the conspiracy of the wicked. He describes the evildoers as sharpening their tongues like swords and shooting deadly words at innocent men from ambush, while encouraging one another in secret snares and asking who will see them. The psalm then turns to say God will shoot them suddenly with an arrow, their own tongues will ruin them, and onlookers will shake their heads. All mankind will fear and declare God's work, and the righteous will be glad in the LORD, take refuge in him, and praise him.

God is asked to hear the psalmist's complaint, preserve his life, and hide him from the wicked. He is shown shooting the wicked suddenly with an arrow, and his work causes all mankind to fear, declare it, and ponder it wisely.

The psalmist, identified in the heading as David, brings his complaint to God and asks to be preserved from fear of the enemy and hidden from the conspiracy of the wicked. He affirms that God will strike down the evildoers and that the righteous will rejoice in the LORD.

l: wicked evildoers (enemies of David), Psalms, Chapter 64
s: The wicked form a noisy crowd that sharpens tongues like swords and aims deadly words like arrows to shoot innocent men from ambush, suddenly and fearlessly. They encourage each other in evil plans and secret snares, asking who will see them, but God strikes them down, their own tongues ruin them, and onlookers shake their heads.

l: righteous (the upright in heart), Psalms, Chapter 64
s: The righteous are described as glad in the LORD, taking refuge in him. The upright in heart are called to praise him.

l: evil plans and conspiracy (the wicked's plot), Psalms, Chapter 64
s: The wicked's conspiracy involves plotting injustice, laying snares in secret, and declaring they have made a perfect plan. The psalm notes that man's mind and heart are cunning, yet the plot is undone when their own tongues ruin them.

l: God's judgment (God's arrow strike), Psalms, Chapter 64
s: God's judgment comes as an arrow that suddenly strikes down the wicked, answering their own arrow-like attacks of deadly words. It leads their own tongues to ruin them, causes observers to shake their heads, and makes all mankind afraid so that they declare and ponder God's work.

Psalm 65, a song of David for the Chief Musician, praises God in Zion as the hearer of prayer who atones for sins and draws chosen people near to live in his courts. It then declares him the hope of the whole earth, including those far away on the sea, who forms the mountains by his power and stills the roaring seas and the turmoil of the nations. People in faraway places are afraid at his wonders. The psalm closes by celebrating his care for the earth: he waters it, enriches it with the river of God, softens it with showers, and crowns the year with a bounty of grain and flocks, so that the hills, pastures, and valleys shout and sing for joy.

God is praised as the one who hears prayer, atones for transgressions, and chooses people and brings them near to live in his courts. He answers by awesome deeds of righteousness, forms the mountains by his power, stills the seas and the turmoil of the nations, and is the hope of all the ends of the earth. He visits and waters the earth, provides grain, and crowns the year with bounty.
Zion is the place where praise waits for God and where vows shall be performed to him.

The speaker confesses that sins overwhelmed them, but God atoned for 'our' transgressions. The one whom God chooses and brings near is called blessed, will live in his courts, and will be filled with the goodness of his house. They are answered by God, the God of their salvation, and perform vows to him.
God's house, his holy temple, is the place where the chosen live in his courts. Its goodness is what those he brings near will be filled with.

The earth is visited, watered, and greatly enriched by God, who drenches its furrows, levels its ridges, softens it with showers, and blesses its crop. Its wilderness grasslands overflow, its hills are clothed with gladness, its pastures are covered with flocks, and its valleys are clothed with grain, all shouting and singing for joy. Those who dwell in its faraway places are afraid at God's wonders.

l: rain and harvest (God's provision), Psalms, Chapter 65
s: God provides grain as he has ordained, using the river of God full of water, drenching furrows and softening the ground with showers to bless the crop. He crowns the year with bounty, and his carts overflow with abundance. The result is overflowing grasslands, flocks on the pastures, and valleys clothed with grain.

Psalm 66 is a song for the Chief Musician that calls all the earth to shout joyfully to God and praise his awesome deeds. It recalls that God turned the sea into dry land and that his people crossed the river on foot, and it says he rules by might and watches the nations. The speakers say God tested and refined 'us' like silver through prison, burdens, men riding over their heads, fire and water, and then brought them to abundance. The psalmist promises to enter God's temple with burnt offerings and to pay the vows made in distress. He then tells those who fear God that God heard his prayer, and he blesses God for not turning away his prayer or loving kindness.

God is praised as awesome in his deeds and so powerful that his enemies submit to him. He turned the sea into dry land, rules by his might forever, watches the nations, and preserves the lives of his people. He tested and refined his people, brought them to abundance, and heard the psalmist's prayer without turning away his loving kindness.

All the earth is called to make a joyful shout to God, sing to the glory of his name, and offer praise. It is said that all the earth will worship and sing to God, and the peoples are urged to make the sound of his praise heard.

The 'us' went through the river on foot after God turned the sea into dry land, and rejoiced in him. God preserved their life and kept their feet from being moved, though he also brought them into prison, laid a burden on their backs, and let men ride over their heads. They went through fire and water and were brought to a place of abundance.

The psalmist vows to come into God's temple with burnt offerings and pay the vows he made with his lips when in distress. He invites all who fear God to hear what God has done for his soul, saying he cried to God and that God listened and heard his prayer. He says that if he had cherished sin in his heart, the Lord would not have listened, and he ends by blessing God.

l: testing and refining of God's people, Psalms, Chapter 66
s: The psalm says God tested his people and refined them as silver is refined. This involved being brought into prison, having a burden laid on their backs, having men ride over their heads, and going through fire and water. The outcome was that God brought them to the place of abundance.

l: burnt offerings and vows, Psalms, Chapter 66
s: The psalmist promises to come into God's temple with burnt offerings and to pay his vows, which his lips promised and his mouth spoke in distress. He specifies offerings of fat animals, rams, bulls, and goats.

Chapter 67 is a song for the Chief Musician, to be played with stringed instruments. The speakers, a community, ask God to be merciful to them, bless them, and make his face shine on them. They want this so that God's way and salvation will be known among all nations on earth. The song calls on all peoples and nations to praise God and sing for joy, because he will judge them with equity and govern them. It closes by noting that the earth has yielded its increase, and that God will bless the community so that all the ends of the earth fear him.

God is asked to be merciful, to bless the community, and to cause his face to shine on them. He is described as the one who will judge the peoples with equity and govern the nations on earth. He is called "our own God," will bless the community, and will be feared by all the ends of the earth.
The peoples are called on twice, in verses 3 and 5, to praise God, with the refrain "Let all the peoples praise you." They are told that God will judge them with equity.
The nations are to come to know God's way and salvation. They are urged to be glad and sing for joy because God will judge the peoples with equity and govern the nations on earth.

The community asks God for mercy, blessing, and the shining of his face on them. They hope that through this God's way and salvation will be known among all nations. They state with confidence that the earth has yielded its increase and that God will bless them.

God's blessing is requested in verse 1 and affirmed in verses 6 and 7 as something God will give to the community. The earth's yielded increase is mentioned alongside it. The blessing is linked to a wider purpose: that God's way be known on earth and that all the ends of the earth fear him.

Psalm 68, a psalm of David for the Chief Musician, calls on God to rise and scatter his enemies while the righteous rejoice. It praises God as father of the fatherless and defender of widows, who sets the lonely in families and freed prisoners, and recalls his march through the wilderness to Sinai and the defeat of kings. God is said to choose a mountain to reign on forever, in contrast to the envious mountains of Bashan, and to ascend on high, leading captives and receiving gifts. The psalm describes a procession of singers and tribal princes into the sanctuary, and looks ahead to kings bringing presents to Jerusalem and Egypt, Ethiopia, and all kingdoms singing to God. It ends by declaring God awesome in his sanctuaries and the giver of strength and power to his people Israel.

God is called to arise and scatter his enemies, and is praised as rider on the clouds, father of the fatherless, defender of widows, and the one who sets the lonely in families. He marched before his people through the wilderness to Sinai, ascended on high leading captives, daily bears his people's burdens, and promises to strike his enemies, and is hailed as awesome in his sanctuaries and giver of strength to his people.

They are asked to be scattered and to flee, driven away like smoke and melting like wax before fire. God will strike through the head of those who continue in guilt, and the nations who delight in war are to be scattered, with kings of armies fleeing.
The righteous are called to be glad and rejoice with gladness before God. In contrast to the wicked who perish at his presence, they are the ones who rejoice.

Israel is God's people, whom he led through the wilderness, whose inheritance he confirmed when it was weary, and whose assembly blesses him. God's excellency is over Israel, and the God of Israel gives strength and power to his people.

l: mountain where God chooses to reign, Psalms, Chapter 68
s: The rugged mountains of Bashan are asked why they look in envy at this mountain, where God chooses to reign and where the LORD will dwell forever. It is linked to the sanctuary and to the temple at Jerusalem, to which kings will bring presents.

l: procession into the sanctuary, Psalms, Chapter 68
s: People have seen the processions of God, the speaker's King, into the sanctuary. The singers went first, minstrels followed among ladies playing tambourines, calling to bless God in the congregations, with the princes of Benjamin, Judah, Zebulun, and Naphtali present.

In Chapter 69, a psalmist attributed to David cries to God for rescue from overwhelming waters and mire, describing exhaustion, hatred without cause, and shame borne for God's sake. He is a stranger to his own family, mocked in the gate and by drunkards, and given poison and vinegar when he seeks comfort. He asks God to deliver, answer, and redeem him, then calls for severe judgment on his persecutors, including desolation and being blotted out of the book of life. He closes by vowing to praise God with song and thanksgiving, and declares that God hears the needy and will save Zion and build the cities of Judah for those who love his name.

God is called on by the psalmist to save, answer, draw near, and redeem him, and is said to know the psalmist's foolishness, sins, reproach, and adversaries. The psalmist asks God to pour out indignation on the enemies and blot them from the book of life. God is said to hear the needy, to not despise his captive people, and to be the one who will save Zion and build the cities of Judah.

The psalmist cries out that he is sinking, weary, and with a dry throat, and that he has borne reproach and shame for God's sake and become a stranger to his brothers. He is mocked in the gate, given poison and vinegar, and finds no comforters. He prays for deliverance, asks for judgment on his enemies, and vows to praise God with a song and thanksgiving, which he says will please the LORD more than an ox or bull.

The enemies hate the psalmist without cause, outnumber the hairs of his head, and are mighty. They mock him, give him poison and vinegar, and persecute one whom God has wounded. The psalmist asks that their table become a snare, their eyes be darkened, their habitation be desolate, and that they be charged with crime upon crime and blotted out of the book of life.

l: deep waters (the psalmist's peril), Psalms, Chapter 69
s: The waters have come up to the psalmist's neck, and he sinks in deep mire with no foothold as the floods overflow him. He prays that the flood waters not overwhelm him, that the deep not swallow him, and that the pit not shut its mouth on him. He asks to be delivered out of the mire and the deep waters.

Chapter 70 is a short prayer headed "For the Chief Musician. By David. A reminder." David urgently asks the LORD to hurry and deliver him and help him. He asks that those who seek his soul and desire his ruin be disappointed, confounded, and turned back in disgrace, including those who say "Aha! Aha!" He asks that all who seek God rejoice and be glad in God and continually say "Let God be exalted!" He closes by describing himself as poor and needy and calling God his help and deliverer, asking God not to delay.

God, also addressed as LORD, is urgently called on by David to hurry, come quickly, and deliver and help him. He is described as David's help and deliverer, and is the one whom those who love his salvation say should be exalted.
David is named as the author of this prayer for the Chief Musician. He pleads for quick deliverance, calls himself poor and needy, and asks that his pursuers be shamed. He asks God not to delay.

David's enemies are described as seeking his soul and desiring his ruin, and as mocking him with "Aha! Aha!" David asks that they be disappointed, confounded, turned back in disgrace, and turned because of their shame.

l: worshippers (those who seek God), Psalms, Chapter 70
s: Those who seek God are the subject of David's wish that they rejoice and be glad in him. They are described as loving his salvation, and David asks that they continually say "Let God be exalted!"

In Chapter 71, the speaker, an aging psalmist, asks the LORD for refuge, rescue, and deliverance from wicked and cruel enemies. He recalls relying on God from his youth and even from the womb, and he begs not to be rejected or forsaken in old age when his strength fails. His enemies conspire, saying God has forsaken him and no one will rescue him, and he prays that they be disappointed and covered with disgrace. He vows to keep hoping and to declare God's righteousness, salvation, and mighty works to the next generation. The chapter ends with the speaker promising to praise God with harp, lyre, and voice, trusting that those who want to harm him will be confounded.

The LORD is addressed as the speaker's refuge, rock, fortress, hope, and confidence, who took him from his mother's womb and taught him from his youth. His righteousness reaches to the heavens, he has done great things, and no one is like him. He is said to have shown many bitter troubles, and the speaker trusts he will let him live and bring him up again from the depths of the earth.

The speaker takes refuge in the LORD, asks for rescue, and pleads not to be forsaken in old age when his strength fails. He recalls relying on God since the womb, calls himself a marvel to many, and resolves to hope always. He vows to declare God's righteousness, salvation, and strength to the next generation and to sing praises with harp and lyre, saying his soul has been redeemed.

The speaker's enemies talk about him and conspire together, watching for his soul. They say God has forsaken him and urge one another to pursue and take him because no one will rescue him. The speaker asks that these accusers be disappointed, consumed, and covered with disgrace and scorn, and states that they are disappointed and confounded.

Praise is the speaker's ongoing commitment: his mouth will be filled with it all day long, and he will add to all of God's praise. He promises to express it by telling of God's righteousness and salvation, and by singing with the harp and lyre, with shouting lips and a redeemed soul. He intends to carry these declarations to the next generation and everyone to come.

Chapter 72, attributed to Solomon, is a prayer asking God to give the king his justice and righteousness. It describes the royal son judging God's people and the poor with righteousness, saving the needy, and breaking the oppressor in pieces. His reign is pictured as lasting as long as the sun and moon, bringing prosperity, peace, and abundant grain, with dominion from sea to sea and kings of Tarshish, the islands, Sheba, and Seba bringing tribute. The king pities and redeems the poor and needy from oppression and violence, and men pray for and bless him, and his name endures forever. The chapter closes with praise to the LORD God, the God of Israel, who alone does marvelous deeds, and ends with a note that these are the prayers by David, the son of Jesse.

God is asked to give the king his justice and righteousness, and the people are said to fear him while the sun and moon endure. The chapter closes by praising him as the God of Israel who alone does marvelous deeds, and by asking that his glorious name be blessed forever and the whole earth be filled with his glory.

The king is the royal son for whom justice and righteousness are requested. He is pictured as judging the people and the poor rightly, breaking the oppressor, ruling from sea to sea, receiving homage and tribute from enemies and kings, and being prayed for and blessed. His name is said to endure forever, and all nations will call him blessed.

The poor and needy are judged with justice by the king, who saves the children of the needy and delivers those who cry out and have no helper. He has pity on them and redeems their souls from oppression and violence, and their blood is precious in his sight.

Justice and righteousness are what the prayer asks God to give the king, and by them he judges God's people and the poor. The hills bring the fruit of righteousness, and in the king's days the righteous flourish with abundant peace.

Chapter 73 is a psalm by Asaph in which he confesses that he nearly stumbled in envy when he saw the prosperity of the wicked, who are arrogant, violent, free from burdens, and who mock God by asking how he could know. Asaph felt that keeping his heart clean had been in vain because he was plagued and punished daily, yet he refrained from speaking this aloud so as not to betray God's children. His understanding changed when he entered God's sanctuary and considered the end of the wicked, whom God sets in slippery places and suddenly destroys. Asaph then admits he was senseless like a brute beast, affirms that God holds his right hand, guides him, and will receive him to glory, and declares God his strength, portion, and refuge. He concludes that those far from God will perish and that it is good to draw near to God and tell of his works.

God is declared good to Israel and to the pure in heart, and is mocked by the wicked who doubt that he knows anything. He sets the wicked in slippery places and throws them down to destruction, and will despise their fantasies when he awakes. He holds Asaph's right hand, guides him with counsel, will receive him to glory, and is his strength, portion forever, and refuge.

Asaph, author of the psalm, confesses that his feet nearly slipped because he envied the prosperous wicked, and that he felt his pure living was in vain amid daily plague and punishment. He held back from speaking this so as not to betray God's children, and found understanding in God's sanctuary, where he saw the wicked's end. He admits he was senseless like a brute beast, then affirms that God upholds him, that he desires no one but God, and that it is good to be near God and tell of his works.

The wicked are described as arrogant, proud, violent, fat and conceited, scoffing and threatening oppression, and speaking against heaven and earth. They deny God's knowledge by saying, "How does God know?" They appear free from struggles and burdens, but in the end they are set in slippery places, destroyed, and those far from God perish.

l: prosperity of the wicked, Psalms, Chapter 73
s: The wicked's prosperity is what stirred Asaph's envy: they have firm strength, no struggles in death, freedom from the burdens others bear, abundant waters, and ever-increasing riches while always at ease. In the sanctuary Asaph learns that this ease is temporary and is likened to a dream that vanishes on waking.

l: destruction of the wicked, Psalms, Chapter 73
s: Asaph understands the wicked's destruction when he enters God's sanctuary and considers their latter end. God throws them down from slippery places, and they are suddenly and completely swept away with terrors, their fantasies despised like a dream on waking. Those far from God and unfaithful to him perish.

In Chapter 74, a contemplation by Asaph, the speaker asks God why he has rejected his people, the sheep of his pasture, and urges him to remember Mount Zion, his congregation and inheritance. The speaker describes how adversaries roared in the assembly, set up their standards, hacked down the carved work with axes and hammers, burned the sanctuary, and burned all the places of worship in the land. The people see no signs and have no prophet, and the speaker asks how long the enemy will blaspheme. Recalling that God is King of old, who divided the sea, broke the heads of Leviathan, and set the day, night, boundaries of the earth, summer and winter, the speaker appeals to God to remember the mockery, honor his covenant, protect his dove and his poor, and arise to plead his own cause.

God is addressed by the speaker as apparently having rejected his people forever, with his anger smoldering, and is asked why he holds back his right hand. He is affirmed as King of old who works salvation throughout the earth, divided the sea, broke the heads of the sea monsters and Leviathan, opened spring and stream, dried up mighty rivers, and made day, night, light, sun, the earth's boundaries, summer and winter. The speaker urges him to remember his congregation and the enemy's mockery, to honor his covenant, to protect the poor and needy, and to arise and plead his own cause.

l: God's people (the sheep of God's pasture), Psalms, Chapter 74
s: God's people are described as the congregation he purchased of old and redeemed as the tribe of his inheritance, the sheep of his pasture. They now see no miraculous signs, have no prophet, and no one among them knows how long the suffering will last. The speaker pleads that God not deliver the soul of his dove to wild beasts, not forget the life of his poor, and not let the oppressed return ashamed but let the poor and needy praise his name.

l: adversaries (enemies of God's people), Psalms, Chapter 74
s: The adversaries roared in the middle of God's assembly and set up their standards as signs. They behaved like men with axes cutting through a thicket, broke down the carved work with hatchet and hammers, burned the sanctuary, and profaned the dwelling place of God's Name. They said in their heart, "We will crush them completely," and burned all the places of worship in the land. The speaker says the enemy reproaches and blasphemes God's name and that foolish people mock him all day, and asks God to remember the tumult of those who rise up against him, which ascends continually.

The sanctuary on Mount Zion, where God has lived, is described as lying in perpetual ruins because of the evil the enemy did in it. Its carved work was broken down, it was burned to the ground, and it was profaned as the dwelling place of God's Name. God is asked to lift up his feet toward its ruins.

l: destruction of the sanctuary, Psalms, Chapter 74
s: The destruction is portrayed as an assault in which adversaries roared in the assembly, set up their standards, and cut and broke the carved work with axes, hatchet and hammers. They then burned the sanctuary to the ground, profaned the dwelling place of God's Name, and burned all the places in the land where God was worshiped. It leaves perpetual ruins, and the speaker uses it as the ground for asking why God has rejected his people and for urging him to act.

Chapter 75 is a psalm of Asaph, written for the Chief Musician to the tune of "Do Not Destroy." The speaker gives thanks to God, whose Name is near, and speaks of God's appointed time to judge blamelessly while holding the earth's pillars firm. The speaker warns the arrogant and wicked not to boast or lift up their horns, since exaltation comes from no direction but from God, who puts down one and lifts up another. A cup of foaming, spiced wine in the LORD's hand is poured out for the wicked of the earth to drink to the dregs. The speaker vows to praise the God of Jacob forever, and declares that the horns of the wicked will be cut off while the horns of the righteous will be lifted up.

God is thanked because his Name is near and men tell of his wondrous works. He chooses the appointed time to judge blamelessly, firmly holds the pillars of the earth, and acts as judge who puts down one and lifts up another. He is called the God of Jacob and is the object of the speaker's praise.
The wicked are told not to boast, lift up their horn, or speak with a stiff neck. They are made to drink the LORD's cup of foaming wine to its very dregs, and their horns are to be cut off.
The righteous are mentioned in the closing verse, where it is declared that their horns shall be lifted up, in contrast to the wicked.

The speaker gives thanks to God and, in verses 2-5, speaks in a voice that announces judgment and admonishes the arrogant and wicked not to boast. He declares he will proclaim forever and sing praises to the God of Jacob, and says he will cut off the horns of the wicked and lift up those of the righteous.

l: cup of wine (the LORD's cup), Psalms, Chapter 75
s: The cup is in the LORD's hand, full of foaming wine mixed with spices. God pours it out, and the wicked of the earth drink it to the very dregs.

l: horn (symbol of pride and strength), Psalms, Chapter 75
s: The horn is something the arrogant and wicked are told not to lift up on high. By the end, the horns of the wicked are to be cut off while the horns of the righteous are lifted up.

God's judgment is to be carried out blamelessly at the time he chooses. It brings down one and lifts up another, since exaltation comes from no earthly direction, and it is shown in the cup of wine the wicked must drink to the dregs and in the cutting off of the wicked's horns.

Psalm 76, a song of Asaph for the Chief Musician on stringed instruments, celebrates God as known in Judah and great in Israel, with his dwelling in Salem and Zion. It describes God breaking the bows, shields, swords and weapons of war, and leaving valiant men plundered and unable to lift their hands. At the rebuke of the God of Jacob, chariot and horse fall into a dead sleep. God is presented as to be feared, pronouncing judgment from heaven so that the earth is silent, and arising to save the afflicted of the earth. The psalm ends by urging people to make and fulfill vows and bring presents to him, noting that he cuts off the spirit of princes and is feared by the kings of the earth.

God is known in Judah, and his name is great in Israel, with his tabernacle in Salem and his dwelling place in Zion. He breaks weapons of war, rebukes the God of Jacob's enemies into a dead sleep, and is described as glorious, excellent and to be feared. He pronounced judgment from heaven and arose to save the afflicted of the earth. He cuts off the spirit of princes and is feared by the kings of the earth, and people are urged to make vows to him and fulfill them.
The valiant men lie plundered and have slept their last sleep. None of the men of war can lift their hands, showing their helplessness before God.

l: God's judgment on enemies, Psalms, Chapter 76
s: God broke the flaming arrows, the shield, the sword and the weapons of war, and at his rebuke chariot and horse were cast into a dead sleep. He pronounced judgment from heaven, and the earth feared and was silent when he arose to judgment to save the afflicted. The wrath of man praises him, the survivors of his wrath are restrained, and he cuts off the spirit of princes.

Chapter 77 is a psalm by Asaph, addressed to the Chief Musician and Jeduthun, in which the psalmist cries to God in a night of trouble and cannot be comforted. He asks whether the Lord will reject his people forever, whether his loving kindness and promise have failed, and whether God has forgotten to be gracious. He then resolves to appeal to the years of the right hand of the Most High and to remember and meditate on the LORD's deeds and wonders of old. He praises God as the one who does wonders and who redeemed the sons of Jacob and Joseph with his arm. The psalm closes by describing the waters, storm and thunder at the sea, where God's unseen path led his people like a flock by the hand of Moses and Aaron.

God is the one to whom the psalmist cries for help, and he is questioned as to whether he will reject forever, withhold compassion, or has forgotten to be gracious. He is praised as the Most High who does wonders, has made his strength known among the peoples, and has redeemed his people with his arm. His way is in the sanctuary, no god is as great, and his path through the great waters left footsteps that were not known.

The psalmist cries to God day and night, stretches out his hand without tiring, and refuses comfort, groaning at the thought of God and being too troubled to speak. He recalls his song in the night, asks searching questions about God's favor, and then resolves to remember and meditate on the LORD's deeds and wonders of old.

l: people of God (sons of Jacob and Joseph), Psalms, Chapter 77
s: The people, called the sons of Jacob and Joseph, are said to have been redeemed by God's arm. They were led like a flock by the hand of Moses and Aaron. The psalmist asks whether the Lord will reject 'us' forever.
The waters saw God and writhed, and the depths convulsed. God's way went through the sea and his paths through the great waters, yet his footsteps were not known.

l: storm (thunder, lightning and rain at the sea), Psalms, Chapter 77
s: The clouds poured out water and the skies resounded with thunder. God's arrows flashed around, the voice of his thunder was in the whirlwind, and the lightnings lit up the world so that the earth trembled and shook.

l: redemption of God's people (the Exodus), Psalms, Chapter 77
s: God redeemed his people with his arm, the sons of Jacob and Joseph. He led them through the sea by an unseen path, like a flock, by the hand of Moses and Aaron.

l: God's past deeds and wonders, Psalms, Chapter 77
s: The psalmist turns to the days of old and the years of the right hand of the Most High as grounds for appeal. He vows to remember and meditate on the LORD's deeds, wonders and work, noting that God made his strength known among the peoples and displayed power over the waters and in the storm.

l: psalmist's distress and doubt about God's rejection, Psalms, Chapter 77
s: The psalmist's soul refuses comfort, his spirit is overwhelmed, and his eyelids are held open so that he cannot speak. He asks whether the Lord will reject forever, whether loving kindness has vanished, whether the promise has failed, and whether God has forgotten compassion in anger. He answers the doubt by turning to remember God's past deeds.

In this contemplation by Asaph, the speaker calls his people to hear a parable so that each generation will teach the next to trust God and keep his commandments. He recounts God's wonders for Israel in Egypt and the wilderness, including the sea split, the cloud and fire, water from the rock, manna and quail, and the plagues, alongside the people's repeated rebellion, disbelief, and insincere repentance. God punished them yet often showed mercy, remembering they were but flesh. After he brought them into the land, they turned to high places and idols, and he abandoned Shiloh and gave his people over to the sword. He then rejected Joseph's tent and Ephraim, chose Judah, Mount Zion, and David the shepherd, who led Israel with integrity and skill.

God performs wonders in Egypt and the wilderness, splitting the sea, leading by cloud and fire, and giving water, manna, and meat. He is angered by Israel's unbelief and punishes them, yet repeatedly shows mercy, remembering they are but flesh. He abandons Shiloh, rejects Ephraim, chooses Judah, Mount Zion, and David, and gives Israel a shepherd.

Israel, God's people, is led out of Egypt like a flock and brought to the land, where the nations are driven out and the tribes settle. They repeatedly tempt and rebel against God, doubting him in the wilderness and later provoking him with high places and engraved images. He gives them over to the sword, but later provides David as their shepherd.
The children of Ephraim, armed with bows, turned back in the day of battle and did not keep God's covenant. God later rejected the tent of Joseph and did not choose the tribe of Ephraim.

l: Israelites (the fathers and their offspring), Psalms, Chapter 78
s: The fathers told the teachings to later generations and received God's covenant and commands, which they were to pass on to their children. They are also held up as a warning, a stubborn and rebellious generation whose hearts were not loyal, and later Israel dealt treacherously like them. God did marvelous things in their sight in Egypt.

Egypt, including the field of Zoan, is the place where God did marvelous signs and wonders before Israel's fathers. It suffers the plagues, including the death of the firstborn, while God leads Israel out and the sea overwhelms their enemies.

In the wilderness God leads Israel like a flock, splits rocks, and brings streams out of the rock for them to drink. It is also where they repeatedly rebel, grieve him, and demand food, doubting that God can prepare a table there.
God rained manna down from the sky for Israel to eat, called the bread of angels, sent in fullness. It was given even as the people doubted he could provide bread.

God sent meat like dust and winged birds like the sand of the seas, driven by the east and south winds and falling in the middle of Israel's camp. The people ate and were filled, but while the food was still in their mouths his anger struck down some of their strongest and the young men.

God's signs in Egypt included turning rivers to blood, swarms of flies, frogs, caterpillars and locusts, hail on vines, sycamore figs, and livestock, and a band of evil angels. Pestilence and the striking of all the firstborn followed. Israel is rebuked for forgetting these deeds.
Shiloh's tent was where God had placed his dwelling among men. After Israel's idolatry and high places, God abandoned it and delivered his strength and glory into the adversary's hand.
God chose the tribe of Judah, in contrast to his rejection of Joseph's tent and Ephraim. It is linked with Mount Zion, which he loved.
Mount Zion is the mountain God loved and chose, where he built his sanctuary like the heights, like the earth established forever. It is tied to his choice of Judah.

God chose David his servant and took him from the sheepfolds, from following the ewes with young. He was made shepherd of Jacob and Israel, God's inheritance, and led them with integrity of heart and skillful hands.

In this psalm of Asaph, the speaker laments that the nations have invaded God's inheritance, defiled the holy temple, and laid Jerusalem in heaps. The bodies of God's servants lie unburied, their blood shed like water, and the survivors have become an object of scorn to their neighbors. The speaker asks how long God will be angry, and calls on God to pour out wrath on nations that do not know him because they devoured Jacob. The speaker asks God to disregard the forefathers' iniquities, to show mercy, to help and forgive for the sake of his name, and to avenge his servants' blood, preserve the condemned, and repay the neighbors sevenfold. The psalm ends with a promise that the people, the sheep of God's pasture, will thank and praise him forever.

God is addressed as the one whose inheritance and holy temple the nations have defiled, and who is asked how long he will be angry and jealous. The speaker petitions him to pour out wrath on the nations, show tender mercy, forgive sins for his name's sake, avenge his servants' blood, preserve prisoners sentenced to death, and repay the neighbors sevenfold. He is called the God of salvation, and the people promise to thank and praise him forever.

The nations have come into God's inheritance, defiled his holy temple, laid Jerusalem in heaps, and left his servants' bodies as food for birds and animals. They are said to have devoured Jacob and destroyed his homeland, and they do not know God or call on his name. They mock by asking 'Where is their God?', and the speaker asks that wrath and vengeance be poured out on them.
Jerusalem has been laid in heaps by the nations that entered God's inheritance. The blood of God's servants was shed like water around it, with no one left to bury the dead.

l: people of God (sons of Jacob and Joseph), Psalms, Chapter 79
s: God's people have suffered the killing of their servants and saints, unburied dead, and imprisonment, and have become a reproach, scoffing and derision to their neighbors. They plead for mercy, asking that the iniquities of their forefathers not be held against them, and for forgiveness and deliverance for God's name's sake. They promise, as his people and the sheep of his pasture, to give him thanks and praise forever to all generations.

Chapter 80 is a psalm by Asaph, set to the tune of "The Lilies of the Covenant," in which the people of Israel appeal to the Shepherd of Israel, the LORD God of Armies, to restore them. They say he has fed them the bread of tears and made them a source of contention to their neighbors, while their enemies laugh. Using the image of a vine brought out of Egypt, planted after the nations were driven out, and spreading from the mountains to the sea and the River, they lament that its walls are broken and it is ravaged, burned, and cut down. They ask God to look down, visit the vine, and put his hand on the man of his right hand, the son of man he made strong. The refrain "Turn us again... cause your face to shine, and we will be saved" recurs in verses 3, 7, and 19, and the people promise to call on God's name if revived.

Addressed as Shepherd of Israel who leads Joseph like a flock and sits above the cherubim, he is asked to shine out, stir up his might, and save. He is accused of being angry at his people's prayer, of feeding them tears, and of breaking down the vine's walls, though he also brought the vine out of Egypt, drove out the nations, and planted it. The people ask him to turn them again, look down from heaven, and visit the vine.

l: people of Israel (God's people), Psalms, Chapter 80
s: The people, called Joseph, Ephraim, Benjamin, and Manasseh, cry out for rescue. They describe being fed the bread of tears, being a source of contention to neighbors, and being laughed at by enemies. They promise not to turn away from God and to call on his name if he revives them.

l: vine (Israel as God's vine), Psalms, Chapter 80
s: The vine was brought out of Egypt and planted after the nations were driven out. The ground was cleared, it took deep root, filled the land, covered the mountains with shadow, and sent branches to the sea and shoots to the River. Its walls are now broken, so passersby pluck it, the boar and wild animals ravage it, and it is burned and cut down.

l: man of God's right hand, Psalms, Chapter 80
s: He is called the son of man whom God made strong for himself. The psalmist asks that God's hand be upon him, and links this to the people's promise not to turn away and to call on God's name once revived.

The plea is voiced through the refrain "Turn us again... cause your face to shine, and we will be saved," repeated in verses 3, 7, and 19 with the divine title growing fuller each time (God, God of Armies, LORD God of Armies). It also appears as requests to save, look down, visit the vine, and revive the people.

Chapter 81, a psalm for the Chief Musician by Asaph, opens with a call to sing aloud to God and to play tambourine, lyre, harp and trumpet at the New Moon, full moon and feast day, which is described as a statute and ordinance for Israel. God then speaks, recalling how he freed his people from burdens in Egypt, answered them in trouble, and tested them at the waters of Meribah. He commands that Israel have no strange or foreign god, reminding them that he is the LORD who brought them out of Egypt. Because his people did not listen and Israel desired none of him, he let them follow their own stubborn counsels. God laments that they do not walk in his ways and says that if they did, he would subdue their enemies and feed them with the finest wheat and honey from the rock.

God is praised as Israel's strength and the God of Jacob, and speaks as the LORD who delivered his people from Egypt, answered them in trouble, and tested them at Meribah. He commands exclusive worship, offers to fill Israel's open mouth, and lets them follow their own counsels when they refuse to listen. He expresses longing that they would listen, promising to subdue their enemies and satisfy them with the finest wheat and honey from the rock.

Israel is called to sing and rejoice, and is told the festival is a statute and ordinance for it. Israel, also called God's people, was freed from burden and delivered, but did not listen and desired none of God, so was left to its own stubborn counsels. God says that if Israel would listen and walk in his ways, its enemies would be subdued and it would be fed abundantly.

l: festival worship (New Moon, full moon, feast day), Psalms, Chapter 81
s: The psalm calls for music with tambourine, lyre, harp and trumpet at the New Moon, the full moon and on the feast day. It states this is a statute for Israel and an ordinance of the God of Jacob, appointed in Joseph as a covenant.

God recalls that he went out over the land of Egypt, removed the burden from his people's shoulder and freed their hands from the basket. He identifies himself as the LORD who brought Israel up out of Egypt, using this as the basis for forbidding foreign gods and inviting Israel to open its mouth for him to fill. The speaker also says he heard a language he did not know when this happened.

Chapter 82 is a psalm of Asaph in which God presides in the great assembly and judges among the gods. God rebukes them for judging unjustly and showing partiality to the wicked, and commands them to defend the weak, the poor, the fatherless, and the oppressed, and to rescue the needy from the wicked. The text says the judged ones neither know nor understand, walk in darkness, and the foundations of the earth are shaken. God declares that though they are gods and sons of the Most High, they will die like men and fall like one of the rulers. The psalm closes with a plea for God to arise and judge the earth, since God inherits all the nations.

God presides in the great assembly and judges among the gods, rebuking them for unjust judgment and commanding them to defend the weak and poor. God pronounces that the gods will die like men, and the psalm ends with a plea that God arise and judge the earth, since God inherits all the nations.
The great assembly is the setting in which God presides and judges among the gods. It is where the charge of unjust judgment and the commands to defend the weak are delivered.

The gods are accused of judging unjustly and showing partiality to the wicked, and are commanded to defend and rescue the weak, poor, fatherless, and needy. They are described as not knowing or understanding and walking in darkness, while the foundations of the earth are shaken. God calls them sons of the Most High, yet declares they will die like men and fall like one of the rulers.
The wicked are the ones to whom the gods show partiality in judgment. The needy are to be delivered out of the hand of the wicked.

l: the weak and poor (the oppressed), Psalms, Chapter 82
s: The weak, the poor, the fatherless, and the oppressed are those whom the gods are commanded to defend, whose rights are to be maintained, and who are to be rescued and delivered from the hand of the wicked. Their need implies they have not been receiving just treatment.

Unjust judgment is the charge God brings against the gods, expressed as judging unjustly and showing partiality to the wicked. It is linked in the text to the gods' darkness and lack of understanding and to the shaking of the earth's foundations.

In this psalm of Asaph, the speaker appeals to God not to remain silent because His enemies are stirring up and conspiring against His people. A coalition of nations, including Edom, the Ishmaelites, Moab, the Hagrites, Gebal, Ammon, Amalek, Philistia, Tyre, and Assyria, plots to destroy Israel so its name is remembered no more. The speaker asks God to treat them as He did Midian, Sisera, Jabin, Oreb, Zeeb, Zebah, and Zalmunna. He asks that they be scattered like tumbleweed and chaff and pursued by tempest and storm like fire through a forest. The psalm ends with the hope that they will be confounded and seek God's name, and will know that the LORD alone is the Most High over all the earth.

God is urgently asked not to keep silent or be still in the face of His enemies' plotting. The speaker asks Him to repeat past defeats of Midian, Sisera, and Jabin and to pursue the coalition with tempest and storm. The aim is that all will know that He, whose name is the LORD, alone is the Most High over all the earth.

Israel is described as God's people and cherished ones, against whom enemies conspire with cunning. The coalition plans to destroy it as a nation so that its name is remembered no more. The enemies also speak of taking possession of God's pasture lands.

The enemies, who hate God, form an alliance with one mind against Him and His people. The coalition includes Edom, the Ishmaelites, Moab, the Hagrites, Gebal, Ammon, Amalek, Philistia, the inhabitants of Tyre, and Assyria, which helps the children of Lot. The speaker asks that they be made like tumbleweed and chaff, confounded, and perish.

l: plea for God's judgment on enemies, Psalms, Chapter 83
s: The psalmist asks God to act against the coalition, citing the fate of Midian, Sisera, Jabin at Kishon, Oreb, Zeeb, Zebah, and Zalmunna. The requests include making them like chaff, pursuing them with tempest and storm, and filling their faces with confusion. The stated purpose is that they may seek God's name and know that He alone is the Most High over all the earth.

Chapter 84 is a psalm by the sons of Korah, written for the Chief Musician, in which the psalmist expresses deep longing for the courts of the LORD of Armies. The psalmist notes that even the sparrow and swallow find nests near God's altars, and declares those who dwell in God's house and those who set their hearts on pilgrimage to be blessed. Pilgrims passing through the valley of Weeping turn it into a place of springs and go from strength to strength until each appears before God in Zion. The psalmist prays for God to hear and to look on his anointed, and states that a day in God's courts is better than a thousand elsewhere. The psalm closes by calling the LORD a sun and a shield who gives grace and glory and withholds no good thing from those who walk blamelessly, and by blessing the one who trusts in him.

The LORD of Armies, also called LORD God, God of Jacob, King, and God, is addressed by the psalmist as the one whose dwellings are lovely and who is asked to hear prayer. He is described as a shield and as a sun who gives grace and glory and withholds no good thing from those who walk blamelessly. The psalm declares blessed the one who trusts in him.

l: dwellings of the LORD (courts and house), Psalms, Chapter 84
s: The dwellings, courts, and house of the LORD are called lovely and are the object of the psalmist's fainting longing. Sparrows and swallows have nests near his altars, and those who dwell there are blessed and always praising him. A day in his courts is said to be better than a thousand elsewhere.

The psalmist longs and faints for the courts of the LORD, with heart and flesh crying out for the living God. He prays for God to hear him and look on his anointed, and says he would rather be a doorkeeper in God's house than dwell in the tents of wickedness. He ends by pronouncing blessed the man who trusts in the LORD of Armies.

l: pilgrims (those whose strength is in God), Psalms, Chapter 84
s: Those whose strength is in God and who have set their hearts on a pilgrimage are called blessed. Passing through the valley of Weeping, they make it a place of springs, and the autumn rain covers it with blessings. They go from strength to strength, and each one appears before God in Zion.

Psalm 85, a psalm by the sons of Korah for the Chief Musician, recalls how the LORD has favored his land, restored Jacob's fortunes, forgiven his people's iniquity, and turned from his fierce anger. The psalmist then asks God of salvation to turn them again, end his indignation, revive his people, and show them loving kindness and salvation. The speaker resolves to hear what God will say, expecting peace for his saints, who must not return to folly. The psalm closes with a vision of salvation near those who fear him, mercy, truth, righteousness and peace meeting, the land yielding its increase, and righteousness going before the LORD to prepare the way for his steps.

The LORD is said to have been favorable to his land, restored the fortunes of Jacob, forgiven his people's iniquity, covered all their sin, and taken away his wrath. The psalmist asks him to turn them, revive them, and show loving kindness and salvation, and expects him to speak peace to his people and give what is good. Righteousness goes before him and prepares the way for his steps.

l: land of the LORD, Psalms, Chapter 85
s: The land is described as having received the LORD's favor. It is the place where glory is to dwell, where truth springs out of the earth, and where the land will yield its increase when the LORD gives what is good.

The people have been forgiven their iniquity and had all their sin covered, yet they plead to be turned, relieved of God's indignation, and revived so they may rejoice in him. God will speak peace to them, his saints, but they are warned not to turn again to folly.

The LORD's wrath is said to have been completely taken away, and he has turned from the fierceness of his anger. The psalmist nonetheless asks that his indignation cease and questions whether he will be angry forever or draw out his anger to all generations.
God is addressed as the God of our salvation, and the psalmist asks the LORD to grant it. It is declared to be near those who fear him, so that glory may dwell in the land.
Mercy is pictured as meeting together with truth. It is part of the vision of reconciliation in verse 10.
Truth meets together with mercy and is said to spring out of the earth. It is part of the psalm's picture of restoration in the land.
Righteousness is said to have kissed peace, to look down from heaven, and to go before the LORD, preparing the way for his steps.
God will speak peace to his people, his saints. Peace is pictured as kissing righteousness.

Chapter 86 is a prayer by David in which he pleads with the LORD to hear him because he is poor and needy. He asks for preservation, mercy, joy, and strength, and declares that the Lord is good, forgiving, and abundant in loving kindness. He praises the Lord as incomparable among the gods, foresees all nations worshiping him, and asks to be taught the Lord's way and given an undivided heart. David says the Lord has delivered him from the lowest Sheol, while proud and violent men have risen against him without regard for God. He closes by asking the Lord to turn to him, save him, and show a sign of goodness so that those who hate him will be shamed.

The LORD is addressed by David as good, ready to forgive, merciful, gracious, slow to anger, and abundant in loving kindness and truth. He is described as great, as doing wondrous things, as God alone, and as having no equal among the gods. David says he has delivered his soul from the lowest Sheol, and that all nations he made will come to worship and glorify his name. David asks him to hear, preserve, teach, strengthen, and save him, and to show a sign of goodness.

David offers a prayer in which he calls himself poor, needy, godly, and the Lord's servant who trusts in him. He asks for mercy, joy, teaching, an undivided heart, strength, and salvation, and he vows to call on the Lord, walk in his truth, and praise him with his whole heart forever. He says the Lord has delivered his soul from the lowest Sheol, and that proud, violent men are seeking his life. He asks for a sign of goodness so his haters will see it and be shamed.

l: the proud and violent men (David's enemies), Psalms, Chapter 86
s: The proud have risen up against David, and a company of violent men have sought after his soul. They do not hold regard for God before them. David asks for a sign of the Lord's goodness so that those who hate him will see it and be shamed.

Psalm 87, a psalm by the sons of Korah and a song, celebrates Zion as the city of God. The LORD's foundation is in the holy mountains, and he loves the gates of Zion more than all the dwellings of Jacob. Glorious things are spoken about the city. The LORD says he will record Rahab, Babylon, Philistia, Tyre, and Ethiopia among those who acknowledge him, each described as born there. The Most High himself will establish Zion, and singers and dancers declare, "All my springs are in you."

Zion is called the city of God, and glorious things are spoken about it. Its gates are loved by the LORD more than all the dwellings of Jacob, and it is said that this one and that one was born in her. The Most High himself will establish her, and singers and dancers say "All my springs are in you."

The LORD has his foundation in the holy mountains and loves the gates of Zion more than all the dwellings of Jacob. He says he will record Rahab, Babylon, Philistia, Tyre, and Ethiopia among those who acknowledge him. He will count the peoples when he writes them up, declaring "This one was born there." He is also referred to as the Most High, who will establish Zion.

The peoples are to be counted and written up by the LORD, who says of each "This one was born there." Named among them are Rahab, Babylon, Philistia, Tyre, and Ethiopia, who are recorded as among those who acknowledge him.

Chapter 88 is a lament attributed to Heman, the Ezrahite, and to the sons of Korah, addressed to the LORD, the God of his salvation. Heman says he has cried to the LORD day and night while his soul is full of troubles and his life nears Sheol. He describes himself as counted among the dead in the pit, afflicted by God's wrath and terrors, and deprived of friends who now find him abominable. He asks whether the LORD shows wonders, loving kindness, or faithfulness to the dead in the grave. The psalm ends without relief, with Heman still crying out, asking why the LORD rejects him, and saying lover and friend have been put far from him into darkness.

The LORD is addressed as the God of Heman's salvation, yet Heman accuses him of laying him in the lowest pit, afflicting him with his wrath and waves, taking his friends from him, rejecting his soul, and hiding his face. Heman asks whether the LORD shows wonders, loving kindness, faithfulness, and righteousness among the dead.
Sheol is where Heman says his life draws near, as part of his description of being close to death and the pit.

l: the dead (those in the grave), Psalms, Chapter 88
s: The dead are described as the slain who lie in the grave, remembered by God no more and cut off from his hand. Heman compares himself to them and asks whether they rise to praise the LORD or whether his wonders, loving kindness, faithfulness, and righteousness are known in the grave, Destruction, the dark, and the land of forgetfulness.
Heman says the LORD has taken his friends from him and made him an abomination to them. At the end he says the LORD has put lover and friend far from him and his friends into darkness.

l: wrath and terrors (God's wrath), Psalms, Chapter 88
s: God's wrath is said to lie heavily on Heman, afflicting him with all the LORD's waves, and his fierce wrath has gone over him. The terrors cut him off, distract him, and came around him like water all day, completely engulfing him.

Heman's prayer is a daily cry, day and night, with hands spread out to the LORD. He asks that it enter the LORD's presence and says it comes before him in the morning, though the psalm records no answer.

Chapter 89, a contemplation by Ethan the Ezrahite, opens by praising the LORD's loving kindness and faithfulness, exalting him above all heavenly beings and as ruler of the sea, Rahab, the heavens, and the earth. It recalls the LORD's covenant with David, his chosen servant, promising him an everlasting offspring and throne, a fatherly relationship, the status of firstborn and highest of kings, and discipline but not abandonment if his children forsake the law.
