The tone then turns to lament: the LORD is accused of rejecting and being angry with his anointed, renouncing the covenant, defiling the crown, ruining strongholds, and letting enemies triumph. The speaker asks how long the LORD will hide himself, reminds him of human brevity and of the reproach borne by his servants, asks where his former loving kindnesses are, and ends with a blessing of the LORD, Amen and Amen.

The LORD is praised as incomparable among the heavenly beings, ruler of the sea who broke Rahab, and creator of the heavens, earth, north, and south, with righteousness and justice as the foundation of his throne. He is recalled swearing a covenant to David and promising never to lie to him or break it. The psalmist laments that he has now rejected and been angry with his anointed, hidden himself, and let enemies prevail, and asks him to remember his former loving kindnesses.

David is called the LORD's chosen one and servant, found and anointed with holy oil, strengthened by the LORD's hand and arm, and promised victory over adversaries, dominion over sea and rivers, and the title of firstborn and highest of the kings of the earth. He is to call the LORD his Father, his God, and the rock of his salvation. The LORD swears by his holiness not to lie to David.

The LORD promises that David's offspring will endure forever and his throne last like the days of heaven, the sun, and the moon. If his children forsake the law and break the statutes, they will be punished with the rod and stripes, but the LORD will not completely remove his loving kindness or let his faithfulness fail.

l: covenant (the LORD's covenant with David), Psalms, Chapter 89
s: The covenant is stated as the LORD's sworn promise to establish David's offspring and throne forever, which he says he will not break nor alter what his lips have uttered. The psalmist later complains that the LORD has renounced the covenant of his servant, in apparent contradiction of this promise.

l: David's enemies and adversaries, Psalms, Chapter 89
s: The LORD promises that no enemy will tax David and no wicked man will oppress him, and that he will beat down his adversaries and strike those who hate him. In the lament, the situation is reversed: the LORD has exalted the right hand of David's adversaries, made his enemies rejoice, and passers-by rob the anointed, while enemies mock the footsteps of the LORD's anointed one.

l: rejection of David's line, Psalms, Chapter 89
s: The psalmist charges that the LORD has rejected and spurned his anointed, renounced the covenant, and defiled his crown in the dust. He says the LORD has broken down his hedges, ruined his strongholds, turned back his sword in battle, ended his splendor, thrown his throne to the ground, shortened his youth, and covered him with shame. The speaker responds by asking how long the LORD will hide himself and where his former loving kindnesses are.

Chapter 90 is a prayer attributed to Moses, the man of God, addressed to the Lord as the dwelling place of his people through all generations. It contrasts the Lord's everlasting existence before the mountains and the earth with the brevity of human life, which is compared to grass that sprouts in the morning and withers by evening. The speaker says people are consumed by the Lord's anger and that their iniquities and secret sins are set before him, so that life of seventy or eighty years is full of labor and sorrow and passes quickly. The prayer then asks the Lord to teach them to count their days and gain a heart of wisdom. It closes with pleas that the Lord relent, show compassion, satisfy them with loving kindness, make them glad for as many days as he afflicted them, show his work and glory to their children, and establish the work of their hands.

Moses is identified as the man of God to whom this prayer is attributed. In this unit he speaks on behalf of the people, confessing their frailty and sin and asking the Lord for wisdom, compassion, gladness and the establishing of their work.

The Lord is addressed as the dwelling place of his people for all generations and as God from everlasting to everlasting, before the mountains and the earth were formed. He turns people to destruction, sets their sins before him, and is asked to relent, show compassion, satisfy them with loving kindness, reveal his work and glory, and establish the work of their hands.

Humanity is told to return and is described as swept away, like new grass that sprouts in the morning and is withered by evening. People are consumed and troubled in the Lord's anger, their sins are exposed before him, and their lives of labor and sorrow end like a sigh. They ask to be taught to count their days and to be made glad.

God's anger is portrayed as consuming and troubling the people, and all their days are said to pass away under his wrath. The speaker asks who knows its power according to the fear due to God, and then pleads that the Lord relent.

Human mortality is shown as brief: a thousand years in God's sight are like yesterday, and life lasts seventy or perhaps eighty years, mostly labor and sorrow, passing quickly as people fly away. The prayer draws from this the lesson of counting one's days in order to gain a heart of wisdom.

Chapter 91 describes the security of the person who dwells in the secret place of the Most High and makes the LORD their refuge. The speaker declares the LORD to be a refuge and fortress, who delivers from the fowler's snare, pestilence, terror, arrows, and destruction, covering the faithful with his feathers and wings. Though thousands fall nearby, harm will not approach the faithful, who will see the recompense of the wicked. The LORD puts his angels in charge to guard and bear them up, and they will tread on the lion, cobra, young lion, and serpent. In the closing verses the LORD speaks, promising to deliver, exalt, answer, honor, and satisfy the one who loves him and knows his name with long life and his salvation.

The LORD is called a refuge, fortress, and God in whom the speaker trusts, and is also called the Most High and the Almighty. He delivers from the snare of the fowler and pestilence, covers with his feathers, and puts his angels in charge of the faithful. In the final verses he speaks, promising to deliver and set on high the one who loves him, answer when called, be with them in trouble, honor them, give long life, and show his salvation.

l: the faithful one (the addressee), Psalms, Chapter 91
s: The faithful one dwells in the secret place of the Most High, rests in the shadow of the Almighty, and has made the LORD their refuge and dwelling place. They need not fear terror, arrows, pestilence, or destruction; no evil or plague will come near them, and they will only look on the recompense of the wicked. Angels bear them up, they will trample the lion, cobra, young lion, and serpent, and the LORD promises to deliver, honor, and satisfy them with long life because they have set their love on him and known his name.

Refuge and protection form the chapter's central theme: the LORD is a refuge and fortress, his wings give shelter, and his faithfulness is a shield and rampart. Protection covers threats by night and day, including the fowler's snare, pestilence, and destruction, and extends through angels who guard the faithful in all their ways and keep them from dashing a foot against a stone. Those who make the LORD their refuge are promised that evil and plague will not come near their dwelling.

Chapter 92 is a Sabbath psalm that declares it good to give thanks to the LORD and praise his name morning and night with lute, harp, and lyre. The psalmist rejoices in the LORD's works and thoughts, which are great and deep, and says a senseless fool cannot grasp that the wicked, though they flourish like grass, will be destroyed forever. The LORD is exalted forever, his enemies will perish and be scattered, and the psalmist has been exalted and anointed with fresh oil, having seen and heard of the enemies who rise against him. The righteous are compared to a palm tree and a Lebanon cedar, planted in the LORD's house, bearing fruit in old age, and showing that the LORD is upright, a rock without unrighteousness.

The LORD is praised for his loving kindness, faithfulness, and great works, and his thoughts are described as very deep. He is on high forever, his enemies will perish, and he is declared upright, the psalmist's rock, with no unrighteousness in him.

The psalmist is made glad by the LORD's work and vows to triumph in the works of his hands. He says the LORD has exalted his horn like a wild ox's and anointed him with fresh oil, and that he has seen and heard of the wicked enemies who rise up against him.

l: the wicked (enemies of the LORD), Psalms, Chapter 92
s: The wicked spring up like grass and flourish, yet they will be destroyed forever. The LORD's enemies will perish and all evildoers will be scattered, and only a senseless fool fails to understand this.

The righteous will flourish like a palm tree and grow like a cedar in Lebanon. They are planted in the LORD's house, flourish in God's courts, and still bear fruit in old age, full of sap and green, showing that the LORD is upright.

l: giving thanks and praise, Psalms, Chapter 92
s: Giving thanks and singing praises to the LORD is called a good thing, to be done by proclaiming his loving kindness in the morning and his faithfulness every night. It is accompanied by the ten-stringed lute, the harp, and the melody of the lyre.

Chapter 93 proclaims that the LORD reigns, clothed in majesty and armed with strength, and that the world he established cannot be moved. His throne is described as established long ago, and he is said to be from everlasting. The floods are portrayed as lifting up their voice and waves, yet the LORD on high is declared mightier than the many waters and the mighty breakers of the sea. The chapter closes by affirming that his statutes stand firm and that holiness adorns his house forever.

The LORD reigns, clothed with majesty and armed with strength, and he has established the world so that it cannot be moved. His throne has stood since long ago and he is from everlasting. He is declared mighty on high, above the voices of many waters and the breakers of the sea, and his statutes stand firm while holiness adorns his house forever.

l: floods (the floods and waters of the sea), Psalms, Chapter 93
s: The floods lift up their voice and their waves, repeated three times in the address to the LORD. The many waters and mighty breakers of the sea make great noise, but the LORD on high is said to be mightier than them.

Chapter 94 is a prayer to the LORD, the God of vengeance, asking him to rise as judge of the earth and repay the proud. The psalmist laments that the wicked boast, crush the LORD's people and heritage, kill the widow, the alien and the fatherless, and claim that the LORD will not see. He rebukes these fools, arguing that the God who made the ear and eye hears and sees, and that he disciplines nations and knows human thoughts are futile. The psalmist describes the blessing of those the LORD disciplines and teaches, and affirms that the LORD will not forsake his people. He testifies that the LORD helped him, held him when his foot slipped, and comforted him, and declares that the LORD, his high tower and rock of refuge, will cut off the wicked in their own wickedness.

The LORD is called the God to whom vengeance belongs and the judge of the earth, and is asked to shine out and pay back the proud. He is argued to hear, see, discipline the nations, teach man and know human thoughts, and he will not reject or forsake his people. He helped and held up the psalmist, is his high tower and rock of refuge, and will cut off the wicked in their own wickedness.

The wicked triumph, pour out arrogant words, boast, break the LORD's people in pieces, and kill the widow, the alien and the fatherless. They say the LORD will not see or consider, gather against the soul of the righteous, condemn innocent blood, and bring mischief by statute. A pit is to be dug for them, and the LORD will bring their own iniquity on them and cut them off.

The LORD's people and his heritage are broken in pieces and afflicted by the wicked, and the widow, alien and fatherless among them are murdered. The text assures that the LORD won't reject his people or forsake his inheritance. Judgment will return to righteousness, and all the upright in heart will follow it.

The psalmist cries out to the LORD for vengeance and asks who will stand up for him against the wicked. He says that without the LORD's help his soul would soon have lived in silence, and that when his foot slipped the LORD's loving kindness held him up. He finds delight in the LORD's comforts and calls the LORD his high tower and rock of refuge.

Vengeance is said to belong to God, and the psalmist calls on him to rise as judge and pay back the proud what they deserve. The text states that judgment will return to righteousness and that the upright in heart will follow it. It is carried out as the LORD brings the wicked's own iniquity on them and cuts them off.

Chapter 95 is a call to worship addressed to a group of speakers and their listeners. The speakers invite one another to sing to the LORD, shout to him, and come before him with thanksgiving, because he is a great God and King above all gods who holds the deep places of the earth, the mountain heights, the sea, and the dry land. They then urge bowing and kneeling before the LORD, their Maker, since they are the people of his pasture and the sheep in his care. The text turns to a warning: the audience should hear his voice today and not harden their hearts as at Meribah and Massah in the wilderness. The LORD recalls how the fathers tempted and tested him for forty years, how he was grieved with that generation of erring hearts who did not know his ways, and how he swore in wrath that they would not enter his rest.

The LORD is described as the rock of salvation, a great God and King above all gods, and the Maker who holds the deep places of the earth and the mountain heights and who made the sea and formed the dry land. He is God of the people of his pasture and the sheep in his care. He speaks of being tested at Meribah and Massah, being grieved forty years with that generation, and swearing in wrath that they would not enter his rest.

The speakers call one another to sing to the LORD, shout aloud, come before him with thanksgiving, worship, bow down, and kneel. They identify themselves as his people and sheep and are urged to hear his voice today and not harden their hearts as at Meribah and Massah.

l: fathers (ancestors of the audience), Psalms, Chapter 95
s: The fathers tempted and tested the LORD at Meribah and Massah in the wilderness, though they saw his work. He was grieved with that generation for forty years, calling them a people who err in their heart and have not known his ways. He swore in wrath that they would not enter his rest.

Worship and praise are the opening and central call of the chapter: singing, shouting aloud, thanksgiving, songs, bowing down, and kneeling before the LORD. They are grounded in his greatness as King and Maker and in his care for his people. The chapter ties them to hearing his voice and not hardening the heart.

Chapter 96 is a call to worship addressed to all the earth and the families of nations. It urges them to sing a new song to the LORD, bless his name, proclaim his salvation, and declare his glory among the peoples. The LORD is described as great, to be feared above all gods, because the gods of the peoples are idols while he made the heavens. The people are told to ascribe glory and strength to him, bring an offering, worship in holy array, and tremble before him. The heavens, earth, sea, field, and trees are called to rejoice before the LORD, who is coming to judge the earth and the world with righteousness and truth.

The LORD is declared great and greatly to be praised, to be feared above all gods, and the maker of the heavens. Honor and majesty are before him, strength and beauty are in his sanctuary, and he reigns, has established the world, and is coming to judge the earth with righteousness and truth.
All the earth is commanded to sing to the LORD and to tremble before him. The earth is also told to rejoice, and it is the object of the LORD's coming judgment.
